title: Two kinds of bread
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever been offered a shortcut at work or school that nobody would ever notice?
options: then this one is for you. listen.
then you’ll know this feeling. listen.
then keep this one for when it comes.

steps.line: In the town of Saidpur, Guru Nanak stayed with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who earned every coin with his own two hands.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: Lalo shared what he had: coarse, plain bread. The Guru ate it gladly.
Across town, a rich official, Malik Bhago, threw a great feast for holy men. Everyone came, except Guru Nanak.

steps.q: Why might Guru Nanak choose a carpenter’s plain bread over a rich man’s feast?
o: He cared how the food was earned
steps.why: Lalo was a low-caste carpenter, and the town was shocked a holy man would eat with him. The Guru cared about honest bread, not rank.

steps.line: Bhago was insulted, and sent for him. Why do you eat a poor man’s bread and refuse mine?

steps.q: The Guru asks for a piece of each man’s bread. What do you think he does with them?
o: Squeezes them, one in each hand
Gives them both to the poor
Eats them both to keep the peace
steps.why: He didn’t argue. He let the bread show where each man’s money came from.

steps.line: He took Lalo’s bread in one hand and Bhago’s rich food in the other, and squeezed.
From Lalo’s bread came drops of milk. From Bhago’s came drops of blood. His wealth had been squeezed out of the poor.

steps.q: Bhai Lalo is named in the Guru Granth Sahib itself. How?
o: Guru Nanak speaks to him in a hymn
He wrote one of its hymns
steps.why: In a hymn about Babur’s invasion, Guru Nanak addresses him by name: “O Lalo.” A poor carpenter is spoken to in Sikh scripture.

steps.line: Sikhs call this kirat karni: honest work. Earn your living by your own effort, without cheating anyone.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Kirat karni is one of three pillars of Sikh life. Which two join it?
steps.why: Naam japna, remembering God, and vand chhakna, sharing with others. Lalo did all three with one loaf.

say: here’s what i love. the guru didn’t care how fancy the food was. he cared what was in it: honest sweat, or someone else’s.
that’s kirat karni, the first of three pillars of sikh life i’ll show you this week. you don’t leave the world to find god. you earn cleanly, right in the middle of it.

steps.q: Bhago’s feast fed many holy men. From the story, why did the Guru still turn it down?
o: It was served too late in the day
Giving can’t clean money taken from the poor
He only ate with working people
steps.why: Giving matters, but so does how you got it. Earn it clean first.

today.say: today, notice one shortcut nobody would catch: a padded hour, a borrowed idea, a fib on a form. and skip it. earn it clean.
options: then that’s where the first pillar stands today.
i believe you. then notice how good plain bread tastes.

card.keepWhy: Earned clean. That’s what makes it sweet.
sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak, Bhai Lalo the carpenter and Malik Bhago at Saidpur (Eminabad)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (“ghaal khaae kichh hathahu dey”: one who eats what they earn by effort and gives some with their own hand recognizes the path)
Sikh teaching of kirat karni as one of three pillars
check: Milk from Lalo’s bread and blood from Bhago’s is a traditional miracle story; labeled. Caption keeps the word “blood”; the painting shows only the milk.
Many tellings say Lalo’s bread was coarse millet (kodhra) and that Bhago repented; neither detail is stated as fact in the captions.
